lead: Reflux is the liquid returned from the condenser to the top of the column, and the reflux ratio R = L/D compares it with the distillate D. R sets the main trade-off of distillation: more reflux needs fewer stages but more reboiler steam and condenser water. At minimum reflux the stage count is infinite; at total reflux it is the smallest possible but no product leaves. Designers work between the two, usually at 1.2 to 1.5 times the minimum, where the total annual cost is lowest.
prereq: You need: 4.1 for α and equilibrium, and 4.4 for McCabe-Thiele operating lines.

sections.h3: Reflux ratio and the operating line

blocks.text: Vapour from the top tray is condensed. Part of the condensate, L, returns to the column as reflux; the rest leaves as distillate D. The reflux ratio is a pure number:

blocks.where: R is the reflux ratio; L is the reflux flow (kmol/h); D is the distillate flow (kmol/h); V is the vapour flow to the condenser (kmol/h).

blocks.text: On the y-x diagram the rectifying operating line has slope R/(R + 1) and intercept xD/(R + 1) (see McCabe-Thiele). Raising R steepens the line toward the diagonal and pulls it away from the equilibrium curve, so each stage makes a larger change in composition and fewer stages are needed. The price is vapour: every extra mole of reflux must be boiled in the reboiler and condensed again, so both duties grow as (R + 1)D.

items: R → ∞ (total reflux): fewest stages, no product.
R = R<sub>min</sub>: infinite stages, least energy.
R<sub>min</sub> < R < ∞: a finite column; the choice is economic.

blocks.text: Lowering R moves the operating line toward the equilibrium curve. At the minimum reflux R<sub>min</sub> the two first touch. At the touch point, the pinch, the driving force y* − y is zero: a stage there changes nothing, the staircase crowds into the corner and never passes it, and the stage count becomes infinite. R<sub>min</sub> is a limit, never an operating reflux.
For an ideal-shaped curve the pinch sits where the q-line meets the equilibrium curve, at (x′, y′). The rectifying line through (x<sub>D</sub>, x<sub>D</sub>) and the pinch gives:

blocks.where: x′, y′ are the pinch coordinates on the equilibrium curve (mole fractions); x<sub>D</sub> is the distillate mole fraction. For a saturated-liquid feed x′ = x<sub>F</sub> and y′ = y<sub>F</sub>*, which rearranges to R<sub>min</sub> = (x<sub>D</sub> − y<sub>F</sub>*)/(y<sub>F</sub>* − x<sub>F</sub>).

blocks.text: For a saturated-vapour feed the q-line is horizontal at y = x<sub>F</sub>, so y′ = x<sub>F</sub> and x′ is the liquid in equilibrium with it. A non-ideal curve with an inflection, such as ethanol-water, can touch the operating line above the feed first: the tangent pinch. Then R<sub>min</sub> comes from the tangent drawn from (x<sub>D</sub>, x<sub>D</sub>), and the feed-point formula gives too low a value.

sections.h3: Total reflux, Fenske, and the optimum

blocks.text: At total reflux no distillate is drawn and all condensate returns, so R → ∞ and both operating lines lie on the diagonal y = x. The staircase then runs between the curve and the diagonal and gives the fewest stages, N<sub>min</sub>. For constant α, Fenske gives it directly:
N<sub>min</sub> = log[(x<sub>D</sub>/(1 − x<sub>D</sub>))((1 − x<sub>B</sub>)/x<sub>B</sub>)] / log α
blocks.where: N<sub>min</sub> is the minimum number of theoretical stages, including the reboiler; x<sub>D</sub>, x<sub>B</sub> are distillate and bottoms mole fractions of the more volatile component; α is the relative volatility.

blocks.text: Real columns need product, so R is finite. The annual cost has two parts that move in opposite directions. The capital charge falls as R rises, because the column gets shorter, but it rises again at high R because the larger vapour flow needs a wider column and bigger exchangers. The energy cost rises in proportion to (R + 1)D. Their sum is U-shaped with a flat bottom, usually between 1.2 and 1.5 Rmin. Below that the stage count climbs steeply toward the pinch; above it, extra reflux buys few stages. Figure 4.5.1 computes the stage count for the worked example at each R and adds a simple cost model. Gilliland gives the same stage count from Nmin and Rmin without a staircase.

figure.caption: Left: the stage count for the worked example, stepped off at each reflux ratio. It falls from infinity at R<sub>min</sub> = 1.444 toward N<sub>min</sub> = 6.43 and is 14 whole stages at 1.3 R<sub>min</sub>. Right: a simple annual cost, one unit per stage plus six units per unit of (R + 1); its flat minimum lies between 1.2 and 1.5 R<sub>min</sub>.

spec.aria: Two plots against R over R min from 1 to 3. Left, theoretical stages fall steeply from very large values near 1 to about 8.5 at 3, above a dashed line at 6.43, with a point at 1.3 and 13.3 stages. Right, a U-shaped total cost curve made of a falling stage cost and a rising energy cost, lowest near 1.3.

examples.question: A binary column has α = 2.5, saturated-liquid feed x<sub>F</sub> = 0.40, distillate x<sub>D</sub> = 0.95 and bottoms x<sub>B</sub> = 0.05. Find R<sub>min</sub>, R<sub>opt</sub> = 1.3 R<sub>min</sub> and N<sub>min</sub> by Fenske, then the number of theoretical stages at R<sub>opt</sub>.
steps: Fenske ratio: (0.95/0.05)(0.95/0.05) = 19 × 19 = 361. N<sub>min</sub> = log 361/log 2.5 = 2.5575/0.3979 = 6.43 stages at total reflux.
Stages at Ropt by McCabe-Thiele: slope 1.878/2.878 = 0.6525, intercept 0.95/2.878 = 0.3301. Stepping as in the McCabe-Thiele example gives 14 stages including the reboiler, feed on stage 7.
Check by Gilliland: X = (1.878 − 1.444)/(1.878 + 1) = 0.151; the Molokanov fit gives Y = 0.505, so N = (6.43 + 0.505)/(1 − 0.505) = 14.0. The two methods agree.
examples.answer: y<sub>F</sub>* = 0.625, R<sub>min</sub> = 1.44, R<sub>opt</sub> = 1.88, N<sub>min</sub> = 6.4; at R<sub>opt</sub> the column needs 14 theoretical stages (13 trays and the reboiler). The table shows the count climbing steeply below 1.2 R<sub>min</sub>.
examples.check:
import math
alpha = 2.5
xF = 0.40
xD = 0.95
xB = 0.05
yF = alpha*xF/(1 + (alpha - 1)*xF)
Rmin = (xD - yF)/(yF - xF)
Ropt = 1.3*Rmin
Nmin = math.log10((xD/(1 - xD))*((1 - xB)/xB))/math.log10(alpha)
X = (Ropt - Rmin)/(Ropt + 1)
Y = 1 - math.exp((1 + 54.4*X)/(11 + 117.2*X)*(X - 1)/math.sqrt(X))
N = (Nmin + Y)/(1 - Y)
print(f"{yF:.3f}")
print(f"{Rmin:.2f}")
print(f"{Ropt:.2f}")
print(f"{Nmin:.1f}")
print(round(N, 1))

traps: Using R<sub>min</sub> as the working reflux: the stage count is infinite there.
Reporting the Fenske N<sub>min</sub> as the stage count at R<sub>opt</sub>; Fenske holds only at total reflux (6.4 against 14 in the example).
Applying R<sub>min</sub> = (x<sub>D</sub> − y<sub>F</sub>*)/(y<sub>F</sub>* − x<sub>F</sub>) to a vapour or two-phase feed; it is for q = 1 only. Use the q-line pinch (x′, y′) otherwise.
Missing a tangent pinch on a non-ideal curve: check that the minimum-reflux line does not cut the equilibrium curve anywhere above the feed.
Rounding R<sub>min</sub> to 1.44 and then multiplying: 1.3 × 1.444 = 1.878, not 1.872. Carry three decimals until the end.

quiz.q: Define the reflux ratio R and write V in terms of R and D.
quiz.a: R = L/D, the reflux flow divided by the distillate flow. The vapour to the condenser is V = L + D = (R + 1)D.

quiz.q: Why does more reflux reduce the number of stages?
quiz.a: The rectifying line slope R/(R + 1) rises toward 1, so the line moves to the diagonal and away from the equilibrium curve. The gap between the two is larger, each step covers a bigger change in composition, and fewer steps reach x<sub>B</sub>.

quiz.q: What is the pinch at minimum reflux?
quiz.a: The point where the operating line touches the equilibrium curve. The driving force y* − y is zero there, so the steps never pass it and the stage count is infinite.

quiz.q: For α = 2.5, x<sub>F</sub> = 0.40 (saturated liquid) and x<sub>D</sub> = 0.95, find R<sub>min</sub>.
Same separation (x<sub>B</sub> = 0.05): find N<sub>min</sub> by Fenske.
quiz.a: Ratio = (0.95/0.05)(0.95/0.05) = 361. N<sub>min</sub> = log 361/log 2.5 = 2.5575/0.3979 = 6.43, about 6.4 theoretical stages including the reboiler.

quiz.q: The same feed (x<sub>F</sub> = 0.40, α = 2.5, x<sub>D</sub> = 0.95) enters as saturated vapour. Find R<sub>min</sub>.
quiz.a: q = 0, so the q-line is y = 0.40. The pinch liquid is x′ = 0.40/(2.5 − 1.5 × 0.40) = 0.2105. R<sub>min</sub>/(R<sub>min</sub> + 1) = (0.95 − 0.40)/(0.95 − 0.2105) = 0.7438, so R<sub>min</sub> = 0.7438/0.2562 = 2.90, double the liquid-feed value: a vapour feed puts more load on the rectifying section.

quiz.q: Why is total reflux not a production setting, and when is it used?
quiz.a: No distillate leaves, so the column makes nothing although it needs the fewest stages. It is used at start-up to stabilise the column, in tests that measure tray efficiency, and as the Fenske limit in design.

quiz.q: Why does the optimum reflux lie near 1.2 to 1.5 R<sub>min</sub>?
quiz.a: Near R<sub>min</sub> the stage count rises steeply (20 stages at 1.05 R<sub>min</sub> against 14 at 1.3 in the example), so the capital cost explodes. Energy cost rises in proportion to R + 1. Far above R<sub>min</sub> each extra unit of reflux saves less than one stage while the reboiler and condenser keep growing. The sum is lowest a little above R<sub>min</sub>, usually at 1.2 to 1.5 times it.

beyond: Not for the exam. Plant design checks the shortcut result with rigorous stage-by-stage simulation, and heat integration or a heat pump can lower the energy price enough to move the optimum closer to R<sub>min</sub>. Search for "Underwood minimum reflux", "tangent pinch" and "energy integration in distillation".
